title: What is the BCG interview process, and how should you prepare?
description: BCG's hiring steps explained: application, online assessments such as the Casey chatbot case, the skill, case and team interviews, and how to prepare.
hook: BCG's process usually runs from an online application to an online assessment (in many offices the Casey chatbot case), then interviews that BCG describes as a skills interview, a case interview and, for client-facing roles, a team interview, typically over two rounds before an offer. Live cases are usually candidate-led, so you are expected to structure, ask for data and drive. BCG calls its interviews a two-way conversation, which is a useful mindset to walk in with.
body:
In this guide

  • The steps
  • The online assessment and Casey
  • The interviews
  • What BCG looks for
  • A worked example of a candidate-led case
  • How to prepare
  • Common mistakes
  • Practice
  • Where to go next

The steps

BCG's careers site lists four stages: application, a skills interview, a case interview and, for client-facing roles, a team interview. In practice, most generalist candidates see something like this, though details vary by office, role and year:

  1. Application through BCG's portal, with your CV and, depending on office, a cover letter and transcripts.
  2. Online assessment, which varies by office. Many offices use the BCG Online Case, led by a chatbot called Casey.
  3. First-round interviews. Candidates commonly report two back-to-back interviews of about 45 minutes, each with some experience and motivation questions and a case.
  4. Final-round interviews with more senior people, such as principals and partners, with less scripted cases and deeper questions about you.
  5. Offer. Prep guides commonly report four to eight weeks from application to decision.

Always confirm your own process with your recruiter; some offices add other formats, such as a written case.

The online assessment and Casey

The BCG Online Case is a single business case worked through in a chat interface. Candidates commonly report it taking around 25 to 35 minutes, with a mix of multiple-choice questions, numerical answers, short written responses and chart reading. It ends with a short recorded video in which you give your recommendation to the client, typically about a minute long.

Unlike live BCG cases, Casey leads you: it asks the questions and you answer them in order, usually without the chance to go back. So it feels interviewer-led. What it rewards:

  • accurate maths under time pressure, with a quick sense check on every answer;
  • reading exhibits fast and picking out only the data the question needs;
  • a crisp spoken recommendation: answer first, two or three reasons, a risk and a next step.

Use only the tools your invitation allows. Online tests and digital cases covers how to practise for this kind of assessment.

The interviews

The skills interview

BCG describes this as a traditional interview exploring your experience, skills and motivation for joining BCG, and your chance to go beyond your CV. Prepare clear stories about leading, working in a team, overcoming a setback and having impact, plus specific answers to why consulting and why BCG. How to prepare your stories.

The case interview

Live BCG cases are usually candidate-led. After the prompt, you clarify, lay out a structure, say where you want to start, ask for the data you need, do the maths out loud and keep proposing the next step until you reach a recommendation. Interviewers will give hints; a good candidate takes them and builds on them. How to drive a case is the core skill here.

The team interview

For client-facing roles, BCG says it assesses problem-solving, analytical and communication skills in a team setting. Treat it as a chance to show you are a good colleague: listen, build on others' ideas, keep the group moving and summarise. How group cases work.

What BCG looks for

BCG's careers site names five qualities: integrity, intellectual curiosity, creative thinking, a collaborative mindset and drive. In a case, curiosity and creativity show in your brainstorms and in asking why a number looks odd. Collaboration shows in how you treat the interviewer: as a colleague working the problem with you, not an examiner to impress.

A worked example of a candidate-led case

Prompt: A grocery retailer is considering launching a lower-priced own-brand line. Should it? (Illustrative numbers.)

Clarify. Is the goal profit, market share, customer retention, or a mix? Say the client wants profit.

Structure. Demand and likely cannibalisation; unit economics; the retailer's capacity to source and stock the line; competitor reaction; execution risks.

Drive. Say where you would start and why:

"I'd first estimate the incremental profit after the sales we lose from our existing products, because that decides whether the idea is worth pursuing at all. Do we have forecasts for volume and cannibalisation?"

Do the maths. The interviewer gives you the data: the new line earns $2 per item and is forecast to sell 500,000 items a year, but 200,000 of those sales would replace an existing product that earns $3 per item.

  • New line profit: 500,000 × $2 = $1.0M.
  • Lost profit on replaced sales: 200,000 × $3 = $600k.
  • Incremental profit: $1.0M − $600k = $400k a year, not $1.0M.
  • Break-even: the launch stops adding profit if more than $1.0M ÷ $3 ≈ 333,000 of the 500,000 sales are cannibalised.

Propose the next step. "So it is positive but sensitive to cannibalisation. Next I'd test how confident we are in the 200,000, perhaps by looking at a similar launch, and then look at competitor reaction."

Recommend.

"Launch the line in a limited set of stores. It adds about $400k a year, but if cannibalisation reaches a third of sales it adds nothing. A pilot will show the real switching rate before we commit nationally."

Compare a weak version: "The new line makes $1M, so yes, launch it." The maths is right, the commercial judgement is missing, and nothing moves the case forward.

How to prepare

  • Start with BCG's own case interview preparation page and practice material, and read its guidance on using AI in your application.
  • Practise candidate-led cases with a partner, including at least one where you get stuck and must recover. How to practise with a partner.
  • For Casey, practise timed maths and chart questions, then record yourself giving a one-minute recommendation and watch it back.
  • Prepare specific answers on why consulting and why BCG, grounded in the work and people you have learned about.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting to be told what to do. In a live BCG case, silence after an answer is a missed chance to lead.
  • Ignoring hints. If the interviewer nudges you towards a branch, take it and say why it matters.
  • Treating Casey like a live case. It does not wait for your structure; it asks specific questions against the clock.
  • A rambling video. Lead with the answer. One minute goes quickly.

Practice

1. A Casey-style question: a market has 12M units a year. The client has an 8% share and sells at $25 per unit. What is its revenue?

Show the answer

Units: 12M × 8% = 960,000. Revenue: 960,000 × $25 = $24M. Sense check: 10% of 12M is 1.2M units, so 8% should be a bit under 1M. It is.

2. In the own-brand case, cannibalised sales turn out to be 300,000 rather than 200,000. What is the incremental profit, and what do you say next?

Show the answer

Lost profit: 300,000 × $3 = $900k. Incremental: $1.0M − $900k = $100k a year, close to zero. Next: "At that level the launch barely pays. I'd look at whether a different price point or range would reduce switching from our existing product, or whether the strategic goal, such as keeping price-sensitive customers, justifies it."

Where to go next

Compare with Bain's process, practise a full candidate-led case from the casebook, and use the chart drills to sharpen your exhibit reading for Casey.
